choices.text: 2 and 7, the length of the whole array
choices.why: That counts from the start of the array. A slice's capacity is counted from its own start, `wed`, which leaves 5.

choices.text: 2 and 5
choices.why: Right. `wed` and `thu` are its length; `wed` to `sun` is how far it reaches, five elements.

choices.text: 2 and 2, since a slice has no room past its length
choices.why: `mid[:5]` printed `fri`, `sat` and `sun`: the room past the length was there all along.

choices.text: 3 and 5, because `[2:4]` includes index 4
choices.why: The second number is where the slice stops, before it: `[2:4]` is indexes 2 and 3.

prompt: `mid` has length 2 and capacity 5. Which of these runs without a panic?

choices.text: `mid[3]`, since index 3 is inside the capacity
choices.why: An index is checked against the length only: the run stopped with `index out of range [3] with length 2`.
Right. Reslicing upwards is legal up to the capacity, and 5 is the capacity.

choices.text: `mid[:6]`, the six days from `wed` onwards
choices.why: There are only five from `wed` onwards: `slice bounds out of range [:6] with capacity 5`.
Index 2 equals the length, and an index must be less than the length.

prompt: A program stops with `panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:8] with capacity 6`. What does that tell you?
hint: Which of the two numbers does this message name?

choices.text: The slice had length 6 and was indexed at 8
choices.why: An index past the length gives `index out of range … with length`. This message is the reslice one.

choices.text: The array behind the slice has exactly six elements in all
choices.why: Capacity counts from the slice's start; the array has six from there and any number before it.

choices.text: Something asked for length 8 from a slice whose array had 6 elements left
choices.why: Right. `[:8]` asked for a length of 8, and from the slice's start its array had room for 6.

choices.text: The compiler missed a constant 8 it should always catch
choices.why: The compiler let `mid[3]` through too: a slice's length and capacity are known only at run time.

prompt: What does `append` do when the slice it is given has no spare capacity?
hint: Nothing in a slice resizes.

choices.text: Extends the same array in place, the way a dynamic array grows
choices.why: An array never changes size. That is the picture section 03 replaces.

choices.text: Panics with `slice bounds out of range`
choices.why: That is reslicing past the capacity by hand. `append` makes room instead.

choices.text: Allocates a bigger array, copies the elements, returns a slice over it
choices.why: Right, and that new slice is why the result of `append` has to be stored.

choices.text: Allocates an array exactly one element longer
choices.why: Two thousand appends changed the capacity only twelve times; the new array is far bigger.

prompt: The capacity went from 512 to 848, where line 341 of `nextslicecap` computes 832. Why?
hint: 832 `int`s are 6,656 bytes.

choices.text: Above 512 the runtime multiplies by a fixed 1.66
choices.why: 848/512 is a coincidence of rounding: the next steps are 1.51 and 1.40, not a fixed factor.

choices.text: The allocator rounds 6,656 bytes up to a 6,784-byte size class
choices.why: Right. 6,784 bytes is 848 `int`s, and `append` uses the whole array it was given.

choices.text: The compiler's 32-byte buffer added room for 16 more
choices.why: That buffer only serves the first elements, and 32 bytes is four `int`s, not sixteen.

choices.text: The loop asked for 848 by appending 336 elements in one call
choices.why: The loop appends one at a time, so lines 329 and 330 never apply here.

prompt: A colleague's test asserts that after five appends to a nil `[]int`, `cap(s)` is 8. What is wrong with it?
hint: Who chooses the capacity, and what does the documentation promise?

choices.text: Nothing: doubling below 256 makes 8 certain
choices.why: The same loop started 1, 2, 3, 4 in one program and 4 in another; the compiler decides the first steps.

choices.text: It tests a choice the compiler and runtime make, which the documentation never promises
choices.why: Right. `append` promises a big enough array and nothing about its size.

choices.text: The capacity after five appends is always exactly five
choices.why: Both captured runs printed 8 at length 5; capacity runs ahead of length on purpose.

choices.text: `cap` counts bytes, so 8 means one `int`
choices.why: `cap` counts elements: 848 elements were 6,784 bytes in the size class table.

prompt: Which of these does `go doc builtin.append` promise? Choose all that apply.
hint: Read the five sentences, not the runtime.

choices.text: With enough capacity, the destination is resliced in place
choices.why: Yes: "If it has sufficient capacity, the destination is resliced".

choices.text: Without enough capacity, a new underlying array is allocated
choices.why: Yes, in those words, which is why the result has to be stored.

choices.text: The new capacity is twice the old one
choices.why: That is `nextslicecap` below 256, an implementation detail; the documentation says nothing about size.

choices.text: The old array is freed as soon as it is copied
choices.why: Nothing says so, and section 05 shows other slices still reading an old array.

prompt: A function receives `buf []byte` from its caller and wants a copy with a newline at the end, without any risk of changing the caller's data. Which is safe?
hint: Which one leaves `append` no room in the caller's array?

choices.text: `append(buf, '\n')`, because `buf` is already a copy
choices.why: The header is a copy; the array is the caller's. With spare capacity, the newline lands in it.

choices.text: `append(buf[:], '\n')`, because `[:]` copies the slice
choices.why: Slicing never copies: `buf[:]` is the same view with the same capacity.

choices.text: `append(buf[:len(buf):len(buf)], '\n')`
choices.why: Right. With the capacity cut to the length, `append` has to copy first.

choices.text: `append(buf[0:len(buf)], '\n')`, as it names the length
choices.why: Two numbers set the length only; the capacity still runs to the end of the array.
